meta.title: The G Form: The Box You Already Own
meta.summary: The G form's twelve pentatonic dots are, position for position, the box most guitarists already know as the minor pentatonic — and what decides whether it sounds major or minor is only the note you resolve to.

What decides which one you're hearing is not the shape. It isn't the fingering, and it isn't the frets — none of that changes at all, ever, for this box. What decides it is the note you keep coming back to, the one a phrase treats as home. Land on
and these five notes sound major. Land on
and the exact same five notes sound minor. The only thing that moved is where you stopped.
C major pentatonic and A minor pentatonic are the same five pitch classes —
. The only thing that decides which one you're playing is the note you resolve to.

The same lick that has always sounded like it belonged over a minor chord will sound, note for note, like it belongs over this one — same fingers, same frets, different note to land on.
Five of these twelve dots are new since
filling in around the seven chord tones that were already sitting in this window. Notice, too, that fret

runs under all six strings here, exactly as it did at the top edge of the A form's window. That shared fret is what an overlap between two neighbouring windows actually looks like, once you know where to find it.

Chapter 2 called this the widest form and the one you never hold whole as a chord — too much stretch for one hand to cover in a single grip. As a scale window it is the opposite: the most comfortable of the five to sit inside and run top to bottom. Two notes on a string doesn't care how far apart the chord tones used to be.
